title: Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Risk
learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Risk.
Choose an appropriate defensive control for Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Risk and state the assumptions under which it works.
Define a safe, reproducible verification step for Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Risk, including a relevant negative or failure case.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 3: Security Principles, Threats, and Standards. It builds practical understanding of Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Risk with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Risk gives you the mental model needed to recognize where a security promise begins and ends. Define the security goal and trust boundaries, connect the topic to a realistic failure mode, and use explicit assumptions and evidence instead of guesswork.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Risk can be understood through this sequence: Name the asset → Identify trust boundary → Choose a principle → Verify with evidence. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 16.1 Threats versus vulnerabilities; 16.2 Threat actors and attack motivations; 16.3 Likelihood and impact; 16.4 Risk prioritization; 16.5 Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE); 16.6 Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE); 16.7 Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Define the security goal and trust boundaries, connect the topic to a realistic failure mode, and use explicit assumptions and evidence instead of guesswork.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Safe reference example: Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Risk
content_blocks.expected_output: A threat record connects an asset and entry point to a control with an observable test.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use synthetic data and test accounts. Revisit assumptions when the data flow, roles, or integrated services change.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Define the security goal and trust boundaries, connect the topic to a realistic failure mode, and use explicit assumptions and evidence instead of guesswork. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Risk”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Risk in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Risk is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Define the security goal and trust boundaries, connect the topic to a realistic failure mode, and use explicit assumptions and evidence instead of guesswork.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
